parts.title: Introduction to the Laws of Indices

blocks.content: Indices (also known as exponents or powers) appear in many areas of maths. They're a way to represent the repeated multiplication of a number by itself.
For instance if we had the number 3 multiplied by itself 5 times, we could represent this as: $$ 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 = 3^{5}$$
There are 4 index laws that you must know and understand, these are:
We will now take a closer look at each of these rules one by one.
Let's consider a term with the form $x^{n}$. When we see terms like this we refer to $x$ as the base and $n$ as the index (or power). Now let's take a look at our first index law!
The product of powers:
If you multiply two expressions with the same base, you add their exponents: $$ a^m \cdot a^n = a^{m+n}$$
So for example if we had $3^3 \cdot 3^4$, this is the same as $3^7$, as given our bases are the same (i.e. 3 in this case), we can simply add the indices (i.e. $3+4 = 7$ in this case).
Pretty straight forward right? - Now let's get some practice!

blocks.content: Now we've seen when we multiply two terms together with the same base that we add the powers, so what about when we divide two terms with the same base?
Well maybe you guessed it already - we simply subtract the indices.
The quotient of powers:
If you divide two terms with the same base, you subtract their exponents $$ \frac{a^n}{a^m} = a^{n-m}$$

Pretty simple, right? So if we have $\frac{7^3}{7^2}$, this would simply be $$7^{3-2} = 7^1 = 7$$ All we do is apply our rule, the bases are the same and we're dividing, so we just subtract the power of the denominator from the power of the numerator, and we're good to go!
Now let's test our understanding by working through the following problems.

blocks.content: So we've seen two cases now! First we saw, when we multiply two terms with the same base, we add the powers, next we saw when we divide two terms with the same base, we subtract the powers.
Now our third index rule is a little different, what do we do when we have a power to a power? - we simply multiply the powers.
For example if we had $(12^3)^4$, this is simply $$(12^3)^4 = 12^{3 \cdot 4}= 12^{12}$$ All we've done is multiply the powers. Nothing complicated. So in general we have the following:
The power of powers
If you take the power of a term which has a power you simply multiply their exponents: $$(a^{n})^m = a^{n \cdot m}$$
Pretty simple, right? Now let's answer some questions to make sure you understand.

parts.title: Law 4: The Power of a Product

blocks.content: Now thinking back to our first law, we saw $$a^n \cdot a^m = a^{n+m}$$ In other words, when we multiplied terms with the same base, we simply added the powers.
However, what happens if we want to take the power of a product of numbers which all have different bases? For instance, what is $(ab)^5$ or $(x^{2}y^{3})^7$ ?
Well we do this using our final index law.
The power of products
The power of a product of two numbers, a and b, is given by $$(a \cdot b)^n  = a^n \cdot b^n $$

In other words, all we do is apply the power to each one of the terms in the product, for instance if we have, $$(5 \cdot 12)^8$$ We can write this as $5^{8} \cdot 12^{8}$. Now there's no better way to improve your understanding than answering questions, so attempt the following tasks:

tasks.title: Just a little warm up
tasks.instructions: Fill in each box, then press Submit.

d.feedback: $9 = 3^2$, so $9^3 = (3^2)^3$. What's that as a power of 3?

hint.content: For the second equals sign: did you know $9 = 3^2$?

solution.content: Apply the power to each factor: $(5 \cdot 9)^3 = 5^3 \cdot 9^3$. Then $9^3 = (3^2)^3 = 3^6$, so $$5^3 \cdot 9^3 = 5^3 \cdot 3^6$$

tasks.title: Let's up the difficulty
tasks.instructions: Fill in each box, then press Submit.

hint.content: Use the fact that $5x = 5 \cdot x$, then the fact that $15 = 3 \cdot 5$, then think back to our first index law 😄

solution.content: $5x \cdot 15y = 5 \cdot x \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot y = 3 \cdot 5^2 \cdot x \cdot y$. Cubing each factor: $$(3 \cdot 5^2 \cdot x \cdot y)^3 = 3^3 \cdot 5^6 \cdot x^3 \cdot y^3$$

tasks.title: Not as hard as it looks!
tasks.instructions: Fill in the box with the simplified answer, then press Submit.

ans.feedback: Cube the 3 as well as the $x^3$.

tasks.title: Apply the rule again & again!
tasks.instructions: Fill in each box, then press Submit.

hint.content: Let $A = x^2 \cdot y^3 \cdot z^4$. Then $(A^2)^3 = A^6$. Now replace $A^6$ with $(x^2 \cdot y^3 \cdot z^4)^6$ and carry on.

solution.content: $$\left(\left(x^2 y^3 z^4\right)^2\right)^3 = \left(x^2 y^3 z^4\right)^6 = x^{12} \cdot y^{18} \cdot z^{24}$$

front.content: You multiply two terms with the same base, like $a^m \cdot a^n$. What happens to the powers?

explanation.content: Dividing terms with the same base subtracts the powers: $\frac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}$.
A power of a power multiplies the powers: $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$.

options.why: Correct: same base, so add the powers.
That multiplies the powers. When you multiply terms with the same base, you add the powers.

back.content: The index laws for multiplying and dividing only combine powers of the same base.
